title: Federal Court Strikes Down Trump's $100,000 H-1B Visa Fee as Unlawful Tax
excerpt: Judge Leo Sorokin ruled the fee exceeded presidential authority, but an administrative stay keeps it in effect as the case heads to the First Circuit Court of Appeals.
body:
A federal judge in Boston has struck down the Trump administration's $100,000 supplemental fee on new H-1B visa petitions, declaring it an unconstitutional tax the president had no authority to impose. The ruling, issued on June 8 by U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin, handed a major legal defeat to the administration's immigration agenda — though the victory may prove short-lived as appeals proceed.

The Ruling

Judge Sorokin sided with a coalition of 20 Democratic state attorneys general who filed suit in December 2025 challenging the fee introduced by Presidential Proclamation 10973. The administration had argued the $100,000 charge was a lawful penalty under the president's authority to restrict entry of foreign nationals deemed "detrimental to the interests of the United States."

Sorokin disagreed, concluding the fee was a tax in all but name.

The judge pointed to the Supreme Court's February 2026 ruling that struck down Trump's emergency tariffs, applying similar logic: the president cannot levy a tax without explicit congressional authorization. Sorokin found the fee violated the Administrative Procedure Act, calling the implementation "arbitrary and capricious" and noting it bypassed required notice-and-comment procedures.

Fee in Limbo as Appeals Begin

The victory was immediately complicated. On June 12, just four days after the ruling, Sorokin granted a partial administrative stay of his own order. The stay reinstated the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services' authority to collect the fee while the government pursues an appeal through the First Circuit Court of Appeals.

The Trump administration formally filed its motion to stay Sorokin's order on June 18, according to court filings reviewed by Bloomberg Law. White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said the administration is "confident" the ruling will be reversed.

"The substance and application of the $100,000 payment reveal that it is a tax, regardless of what the payment is called."

— Judge Leo Sorokin, U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts

For now, employers must continue paying the $100,000 fee on qualifying H-1B petitions involving consular processing. The fee applies specifically to new petitions filed on or after September 21, 2025 — not to renewals or workers already in the United States on student visas.

Chilling Effect on Applications

Before the proclamation, employers typically paid between $2,000 and $5,000 in total H-1B petition fees. The 50-fold increase triggered immediate chaos. Court filings showed that as of February 15, 2026, USCIS had received just 85 payments of the $100,000 fee — a fraction of the tens of thousands of petitions the program typically processes.

States argued in their lawsuit that the fee made it prohibitively expensive to hire foreign workers for critical roles. Schools struggling to recruit teachers and rural hospitals unable to attract doctors were hit particularly hard, the plaintiffs contended.

What It Means for Indian Workers

The ruling carries outsized significance for the Indian diaspora. Indian nationals receive nearly three-quarters of all H-1B approvals, making them by far the program's largest beneficiaries. The fee directly threatened the pipeline of talent from India to American technology companies, hospitals, and universities.

Major Indian IT services firms — Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, and HCL Technologies — rely heavily on H-1B visas to place engineers and consultants at American client sites. For these companies, the $100,000-per-petition cost represented a potentially existential threat to their U.S. staffing models. An estimated 730,000 current H-1B holders and 550,000 dependants in the United States stand to be affected by the policy's ultimate outcome.

Three Courts, Three Possible Outcomes

The legal landscape extends well beyond Boston. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce has a separate lawsuit pending in federal court in Washington, D.C., where a judge previously rejected its challenge — a ruling now under appeal. A third suit, filed by religious groups and labor organizations, is underway in federal court in San Francisco.

The three cases set up the possibility of divided rulings across appellate circuits, a scenario that could push the issue toward the Supreme Court. The fee is scheduled to expire in September 2026 under the original proclamation, adding a ticking clock to the legal battle.

Immigration attorneys advise employers to treat the fee as enforceable for the time being, while monitoring court filings for any sudden changes. The First Circuit's decision on the stay — expected in the coming weeks — will determine whether Sorokin's nationwide ruling takes effect or remains frozen during the full appeal process.
